blocks.p: Mercy Office, Abundance. Routing slip, the noon change.

HALE, Stephen. Born: Earth. Residence: none registered. Apparent age: past seventy. Taken: the Bounty Market, lower tier, on the report of a patron. Renewal: gift not received. Effects: one cloth bag, to be reviewed at intake; anything written, reclaimed. Route: Serenity, the holding house, then the Hall. Flag: from Sion, standing. No petition to be entertained.
No one in Abundance had seen an old man in forty years.

Sol Tarren saw him first, though afterward he could not have said why his eyes went there. The Bounty Market at midday was built to hold the eye elsewhere. It ran the length of the great dome in three tiers of glass and brass, and every stall was lit from beneath so that the fruit seemed to glow on its own: Europa melons pale as moons, pyramids of Titan oranges grown under lamps, cuts of real meat hung in cold cases like jewelry. Music came from nowhere in particular. People moved through it all slowly, the way people move through a dream they have had many times and still enjoy, touching things, wanting them, buying them, wanting the next. Sol had always loved this hour.
The old man was standing by a spice stall with a cloth bag held against his chest.

His hair was white. Not silver at the temples in the fashionable way, but white all through and thin, and his face had fallen in the way faces did in the archival images: lines around the mouth, loose skin under the jaw, brown spots on the backs of his hands. He stood a little bent, as if the gravity of Mars, which was nothing, were too much for him.

People had noticed. Sol watched it move through the crowd like a draft through a room. A woman with a child stopped and turned the child’s face away. Two young men who might have been three hundred years old stared openly and then laughed and walked on. The spice seller had stepped back from his own counter. No one said the word, but Sol could see it in their faces: denied. A dissenter refused Renewal and left to age where everyone could see him, so that everyone would remember what the gift was worth.

“Your Grace.” Deacon Pell had come up at his elbow with the morning’s tablets. “The colony administrator has moved our meeting to tomorrow, after the ascension, if that suits. They’ve pulled the ascension records you asked for. Seventeen failures in the inner colonies since the spring, four of them here.” He followed Sol’s gaze and lowered his voice. “Ah. I’m sorry you had to see that.”
“Do you know him?”
“No, Your Grace. I can find out.” Pell touched his temple, where his Halo sat under the skin like a coin. “He’ll be in the compliance registry. They usually are.”
“Don’t,” Sol said, and was surprised to hear himself say it.

He did not know why he had said it. He knew the doctrine as well as any man alive; he had helped to teach it. Renewal was a gift, and a gift could be refused, and a man who refused it chose the old road down into dust. The church did not punish him. It simply let him have what he had chosen. There was mercy in that, and a kind of dignity, and there was a lesson for everyone who passed him in the street. Sol believed all of it.
And yet he found he did not want this man’s name in Pell’s tablet. He wanted to go and speak to him. He wanted, absurdly, to ask him what it was like.
The pressure behind his left eye had come back.

It had been visiting him for a month now, always in the same place, a thumb pressed gently from inside. It never quite became pain. It came, and stayed awhile, and went, and sometimes when it went it seemed to take a little time with it. Twice he had found himself standing somewhere without remembering walking there: once at the window of his rooms in Concord, looking out at Jupiter with his hand on the glass; once in a corridor on Serenity, outside a door he did not recognize, with Pell calling his name from the end of the hall. A minute gone, perhaps two. This morning it had been twelve.
“Your Grace?”
“Nothing.” He pressed two fingers above his eyebrow. “The light in here.”

“It is very bright,” Pell agreed, though it was not, particularly. Pell agreed with most things, and in sixty years Sol had never known him unhappy. Sol envied him that sometimes, without being able to say exactly what he was envying.

The old man had begun to walk. He came along the lowest tier slowly, the bag held against him, and the crowd made way for him without seeming to, the way water makes way for a stone. He was coming toward them. Sol saw it with a strange certainty before it was possible to see it: the man was not wandering. He was looking for something, and his eyes moved over the faces of the crowd one by one, and then they moved over Sol’s face, and stopped.

It was not the look Sol was used to. He had been a bishop of Life for longer than most people in that market had been alive, and he knew the ways people looked at a bishop: with reverence, with hunger, with the bright expectant gratitude of the faithful. Some people looked at him the way they looked at the Pearl in their homes, as if he might grant them something. He knew every one of those looks, and if he was honest he had never tired of any of them. This man looked at him as if he were remembering him.
Then the old man’s face changed. Something went out of it, or came into it, Sol could not tell which. His eyes widened and fixed on nothing. His mouth opened.
He cried out once, a strange high cry, as if the air were being pressed out of him, and fell.

In Mars gravity a man does not fall the way he falls on Earth. He goes down slowly, almost gently, as if he were lying down to sleep, and so for a moment no one understood. Then his body went rigid on the tiles. His back arched. His arms locked against his chest around the cloth bag, and his head pressed back, and a sound came out of his throat that did not sound like a person at all.
Then the jerking began.

It was terrible to watch in the light gravity. Each spasm lifted him a little from the floor, and he came down a little later than he should have, so that his whole body seemed to be fighting something invisible that kept throwing him into the air. A basket of saffron went over. Someone screamed. And then, from somewhere along the tier, a man’s voice said the word everyone had been thinking.
“Virus.”

The crowd broke. It did not run; people in Abundance did not run. But it pulled back from the old man in a widening ring, the way a crowd pulls back from fire, and the mothers covered their children’s ears, because everyone knew it was not the seizure you had to fear. It was what they said afterward. Sol saw a young woman at the edge of the ring touch her temple with two fingers and turn away to speak quietly into her Halo. He knew what she was saying. Mercy Office. The Bounty Market, lower tier. Come quickly.
He was already kneeling.
“Your Grace!” Pell’s voice cracked. “Your Grace, please, the wardens are trained for this, you mustn’t...”

“It isn’t passed by touch, Deacon. You know the catechism.” Sol pushed the spilled basket away from the man’s head with one hand and took off his own outer robe with the other. He folded it and slid it under the man’s skull, so that it would stop striking the tiles. “Clear the space. Don’t hold him down. Nothing in his mouth.” He found he knew the steps without having to think of them, though he could not remember learning them. “Note the time.”
“The time, Your Grace?”
“When it began. They’re shorter than they look.”

They were. It felt like a long while, and Sol knelt through it with his left hand flat on the floor beside the man’s head, not touching him, only there. The church taught that the infected were not to blame. They were sick, and the sickness was in the mind, where no physician could reach it; and so the Mercy Office would take them, and in time release them, gently, up into the City of the Throne, where the Face itself would mend what no one on any world could mend. Sol had preached that a hundred times. He had signed custody orders for more of the infected than he could count, and he had always asked that they be handled gently, and he had always believed they were.

The spasms slowed. They came further apart, then stopped. The old man lay on his side on Sol’s folded robe, breathing in long hoarse pulls, his eyes half open and unseeing. A thread of blood ran from the corner of his mouth where he had bitten his tongue. Sol turned him a little further onto his side, so the blood would run out and not down.
The ring of people held its distance. The music went on overhead, bright and sourceless.
Then the old man began to speak.

It was barely a voice at first, a slur of breath, and Sol had to lean down to hear it. The words came slowly and out of order, the way words come out of someone who has not yet remembered where he is. But they were words, and Sol heard them.
“In the beginning,” the old man said, “was the Word.”
Sol went still.
“And the Word was with God. And the Word...” A long breath. “...was God.”

Everyone in Abundance knew how the Book of Life began. Children learned it before they could read. In the beginning was Life, and Life was the light of all people. Sol had sung it over the cradle of every infant he had ever haloed. This was the same shape, the same rhythm, as if someone had taken the first line of scripture and set a different word in the middle of it like a stone in a ring. The Word. He did not know what it meant. A word was a thing you said. How could a word be in the beginning? How could it be God?
And yet the sound of it went into him and stayed there, the way a splinter does.
“All things were made through him,” the old man whispered, “and without him was not anything made that was made. In him was life...”
“Your Grace.” Pell was standing well back, his face white. “Your Grace, you shouldn’t listen. That’s how it spreads.”
“...and the life was the light of men. The light shines in the darkness...”

The old man’s eyes cleared. Sol watched it happen: the drifting gaze found the brass rail, the spilled saffron, the dome’s gold light, and then it found Sol’s face a hand’s width away, and it stopped there and held.
It was the look from before. Not reverence. Recognition.
“Sol,” the old man said.

No one called him that. Not the Hierarch, not Pell, not even Aurelian, who had known him longer than anyone alive. To the faithful he was Your Grace, to his brothers in the episcopate he was Tarren, and to everyone else he was the bishop. He had not heard his own first name spoken aloud in so long that for a moment it did not sound like a name at all.
“You came,” the old man said. His voice was thick and tired, and he smiled with his bloody mouth. “I hoped it would be you.”
His eyes moved then, slowly, the way eyes move in someone not yet wholly back, down from Sol’s face to the hand on the tiles beside his head, and rested there.
“You still have the burn,” he said.

Sol looked at his own hand. It was only the old scar, the thin shining line across the base of his thumb. The man’s face had lain a hand’s width from it all through the seizure. A mind coming back to itself named whatever was in front of it; Sol had sat by enough beds to know that. It was a patient’s guess, and a good one, and nothing more. Only the word still would not lie down, and he had no time to wonder at it, because the wardens had arrived.

They came down the tier in white, four of them, moving quickly but without hurry, the way the Mercy Office always moved. Their faces were calm and kind. The crowd parted for them with something like relief. The senior warden saw Sol kneeling on the floor in his shirtsleeves and stopped short and bowed.
“Your Grace. We weren’t told a bishop was present.”
“I was passing.” Sol stood. His knees ached; he had been kneeling longer than he thought. “He’s had a seizure. He’s coming out of it now. He bit his tongue. He’ll be confused for a while.”

“Thank you, Your Grace. We’ll take it from here.” The warden knelt by the old man and spoke to him softly, the way you would speak to a frightened animal, while the others unfolded a stretcher. One of them reached for the cloth bag.
The old man’s arms closed around it.
“He’ll keep his belongings,” Sol said.
The warden looked up. “Your Grace, it’s procedure. Anything they’re carrying may be...”

“He’s a patient, not a prisoner.” Sol heard the authority come into his own voice, the voice he used in the cathedral, and saw the warden hear it too. “He keeps his things. I’ll take custody myself. Where will he be held?”
“On Serenity, Your Grace. For assessment, and then Mercy.”

“Then I’ll see him on Serenity.” Sol touched his temple, and his Halo opened the custody form in the corner of his sight, and he signed it with a thought, as he had signed a thousand of them. Received into Mercy by the hand of Sol Tarren, Bishop of Life. “See that he’s comfortable.”
“Of course, Your Grace.”

They lifted the old man onto the stretcher. He did not resist. His eyes followed Sol the whole time, and as they carried him past, he said something too quiet for anyone else to hear, and Sol, who was not sure afterward that he had heard it either, thought it was: Don’t be afraid.
Then he was gone up the tier in a knot of white, and the crowd closed behind him.

It took less than a minute. Sol stood and watched it happen. The ring of people loosened and broke and became shoppers again. Someone righted the saffron basket. The spice seller came out from behind his counter with a cloth and wiped the tiles where the old man had lain, and the blood came up easily, and he went back to his customers. A child laughed. The music had never stopped. Within a minute there was no sign that anything had happened at all, and no one in the whole bright market looked troubled, or sorry, or afraid.
That was the gift, Sol reminded himself. That was what four hundred years of mercy had made: a people with no tears.
“Remember the Mountain, Your Grace,” Pell said softly. He had come up beside him with Sol’s robe, which he had retrieved from the floor and was holding at arm’s length.
“And forget the tears,” Sol answered. The words came by themselves, as they always did.

He took the robe. There was a small dark stain on the collar where the old man’s head had lain. He looked at it for a long moment. Then the pressure came back behind his left eye, gently, as it had by the spice stall, and the light of the market went very bright, and then...
...and then he was standing on the transit platform at the edge of the dome, alone, with his robe folded over his arm and the red Martian afternoon outside the glass.
He did not remember walking there. He did not know where Pell had gone. The platform clock said a quarter of an hour had passed, and he could not account for a minute of it.

What he did remember, with perfect clarity, was the old man’s voice saying a word that had been in the beginning, a word that was with God and was God. And he remembered his own name in that voice, spoken the way no one had spoken it in four hundred years.
As if they were friends.
